overview.title: Bag-of-words vs. sequences, and downloading raw IMDb
overview.main_topic: Why both set (bag-of-words) and sequence models still matter, and how to download and inspect the raw IMDb review dataset
overview.central_idea: Early NLP mostly used order-discarding bag-of-words models, while sequence models came back around 2015 with RNNs; both are still useful. The chapter will compare them on the raw IMDb sentiment dataset, which is downloaded with `keras.utils.get_file` and laid out as train/test folders with `pos/`, `neg/` and an unlabeled `unsup/` directory.
overview.importance: This page moves from the abstract question of how to represent word order to a hands-on, realistic pipeline. Every model in the rest of chapter 14 (bag-of-words, bigrams, RNNs, embeddings), and the Transformer fine-tuning in chapter 15, starts from the directory structure set up here.
learning_objectives: Explain the historical split between bag-of-words (set) models and sequence models in NLP
Download and extract a dataset archive with `keras.utils.get_file`
Describe the folder layout of the raw aclImdb dataset and what `pos/`, `neg/` and `unsup/` contain
Explain why you should look at raw samples before building a model
prerequisites: The prevectorized IMDb dataset from chapter 4 (p.130)

summary:
The page finishes the introduction to **section 14.3, Sets vs. sequences**, and starts the practical work.

**Historical context.** Most early machine-learning work on natural language used **bag-of-words** models, which treat a text as an unordered set of tokens and so throw away word order. Interest in **sequence models**, which do use order, only took off around **2015, with the rebirth of RNNs**. The authors say both approaches are still relevant today, and the coming sections show how each works and when to choose which.

**The benchmark.** Both approaches will be tested on the **IMDb movie-review sentiment-classification** dataset. In chapters 4 and 5 you used a *prevectorized* version, where reviews were already lists of integer word indices (p.130). Now you start from the **raw text files**, as you would on a new real-world text-classification problem.

**Listing 14.8** imports `os`, `pathlib`, `shutil` and `random` (used on the next page to copy files into a validation split), then calls `keras.utils.get_file` with the Stanford URL of `aclImdb_v1.tar.gz`, `fname="imdb"` and `extract=True`. The function downloads, caches and extracts the archive under `~/.keras/datasets/`. Appending `"aclImdb"` to the returned path gives `imdb_extract_dir`.

The page then lists the directories two levels deep using `glob("*/*")`:

- `train/pos`, `train/neg`, `train/unsup`
- `test/pos`, `test/neg`

Reviews with a **low** IMDb user rating are in `neg/`, and those with a **high** rating are in `pos/`. The `unsup/` (unsupervised) directory holds reviews that the dataset's creator **deliberately left unlabeled**, so each could be positive or negative. They are ignored for now, but section 14.5.4 uses them for pretraining word embeddings (p.438).

The page ends with a general methodological point: **look at your data before you start modeling**. Seeing what the inputs really are gives you intuition for what the model is actually doing. The next page (p.421) prints one review to do exactly this.

paragraphs.excerpt: Historically, most early applications of machine learning to NLP just involved bag-of-words
paragraphs.what_it_says: Early ML for NLP mostly used bag-of-words models, which discard sequence information. Interest in sequence models only grew from 2015, with the rebirth of RNNs. Both approaches are still relevant, and the book will show how each works and when to use which.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This answers the question raised on the previous page (p.419), how to encode token order, with a pragmatic 'it depends'. The simplest option is not to encode order at all (a set model). The other option is to process tokens in order (a sequence model). Neither has fully replaced the other.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This sets up the experimental structure of the chapter: section 14.4 (set models: bag-of-words, then bigrams) against section 14.5 (sequence models: RNN, then embeddings). It also suggests that a cheap, order-agnostic baseline can be competitive, which the experiments will show.
paragraphs.technical_idea: A bag-of-words representation maps a document to a fixed-size vector indexed by vocabulary entries (presence flags, counts or TF-IDF weights). It is invariant to permutations of the tokens. A sequence model takes an ordered tensor of shape (sequence_length,) of token ids and can learn order-dependent patterns.

terminology.meaning: A text representation that keeps which tokens occur (and possibly how often) but discards their order.
A model that consumes tokens in order and can therefore use word order, such as an RNN or a Transformer.
The renewed success of recurrent networks (especially LSTMs) in NLP from around 2015, after earlier work in the 1990s.

connections: p.419: section 14.3 opened by asking how to encode the ordering of tokens in text
p.422: section 14.4 begins the set (bag-of-words) models
p.429: section 14.5 begins the sequence models

paragraphs.excerpt: We will demonstrate each approach on a well-known text classification benchmark
paragraphs.what_it_says: Both approaches will be demonstrated on the IMDb movie-review sentiment-classification dataset. Chapters 4 and 5 used a prevectorized version; now the raw IMDb text will be processed as you would in a new real-world text-classification problem.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The task, binary sentiment classification, is the same as in chapter 4, but the preprocessing work is no longer done for you. You have to read files, build labels from folder names, split off validation data, tokenize and vectorize.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Using a familiar task means that changes in accuracy come from representation and architecture choices, not from a new problem. Working from raw text also teaches the pipeline you actually need in practice, where no `load_data()` helper exists.
paragraphs.technical_idea: The chapter 4 version (`keras.datasets.imdb.load_data(num_words=10000)`) returned integer sequences with a fixed vocabulary. Here the vocabulary, tokenization and output mode become choices you make yourself, typically with a `TextVectorization` layer.

terminology.meaning: Already converted from text to numeric form (here, integer word indices) before you receive it.
Predicting the attitude of a text, here whether a review is positive or negative.

connections: p.130: chapter 4 loaded the packaged, integer-encoded IMDb dataset (25,000 train and 25,000 test reviews, 50/50 balanced)
p.482: chapter 15 reuses this chapter's IMDb loading code unchanged to fine-tune RoBERTa

paragraphs.excerpt: To begin, let’s download and extract our dataset.
paragraphs.what_it_says: This line introduces Listing 14.8, which downloads and extracts the data.
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the first concrete step of the raw-text pipeline.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Downloading through Keras's cache utility makes the code reproducible and avoids downloading the archive again on later runs.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s list out our directory structure:
paragraphs.what_it_says: This line introduces a short interactive snippet that prints the subdirectories of the extracted dataset.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Before reading any files, you check how the data is organized on disk.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The directory layout carries the labels (`pos`/`neg`), so understanding it is a prerequisite for `text_dataset_from_directory` on the next page.
connections: p.421: text_dataset_from_directory infers labels from exactly this kind of folder structure

paragraphs.excerpt: We can see both a train and test set with positive and negative examples.
paragraphs.what_it_says: The dataset has train and test sets, each with positive and negative examples. Low-rated reviews were sorted into `neg/` and high-rated reviews into `pos/`. There is also an `unsup/` (unsupervised) directory of reviews the creator deliberately left unlabeled; they could be positive or negative.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Labels are encoded by folder membership, not stored in a separate label file. The labels are derived from star ratings, so 'sentiment' here really means 'a high or low rating'. Only the training split has an `unsup/` folder.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The `unsup/` folder must be excluded when building a labeled dataset. Otherwise a directory-based loader would treat it as a third class. The next page removes it from consideration. Its 25,000 reviews are not wasted: section 14.5.4 uses them as extra text for pretraining a word embedding (p.438).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Directory-as-label is a common convention in Keras (`image_dataset_from_directory` in chapter 8, `text_dataset_from_directory` here): each subdirectory name becomes a class, in alphanumeric order.

terminology.meaning: Short for unsupervised: reviews with no sentiment label.
Examples without targets. They are not usable for supervised training directly, but useful for unsupervised or self-supervised pretraining.

p.438: the unsup/ reviews are used to pretrain an Embedding

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s look at the content of a few of these text files.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Next, the authors look at a few text files and recommend always inspecting your data, text or images, before modeling, because it grounds your intuition about what the model is actually doing.
paragraphs.what_it_means:
This is a general habit of good practice, not only an IMDb step. Reading raw samples shows you noise (HTML tags like `
`, odd punctuation, very long reviews) and how hard the task really is.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Many modeling bugs are data bugs: wrong labels, leftover markup, encoding problems. Seeing a raw review also explains later choices, such as standardization and the sequence-length cutoff.

concepts.name: Bag-of-words (set) model
concepts.definition: A text model whose input representation records which tokens occur in a document but not their order.
concepts.intuition: Cut every word out of a review, throw the pieces in a bag and shake it. You can still tell that 'terrible', 'boring' and 'waste' are in there.
concepts.technical: A document becomes a vocabulary-sized vector (multi-hot, counts or TF-IDF), which is fed to a dense classifier. The representation is permutation-invariant.
concepts.significance: On this page it is described as the historically dominant approach and one of two families still relevant today. Section 14.4 trains one on IMDb.
concepts.example: 'not good, quite bad' and 'not bad, quite good' map to the same unigram bag.
concepts.misconception: That discarding order makes it useless. For many classification tasks, word presence alone carries most of the signal.

concepts.name: Sequence model
concepts.definition: A model that processes tokens in order and can use word order, for example an RNN or a Transformer.
concepts.intuition: Reading a sentence left to right instead of glancing at a word cloud.
concepts.technical: The input is an integer tensor of shape (batch, sequence_length), usually embedded into (batch, sequence_length, embedding_dim) and processed by recurrent or attention layers.
concepts.significance: The page dates the rise of interest in these models to 2015, with the rebirth of RNNs. Section 14.5 trains one.
concepts.example: An LSTM reading 'not good' can learn that 'not' flips the meaning of the word after it.
concepts.misconception: That sequence models always beat bag-of-words on classification. The book presents both as relevant, and the choice depends on the problem.

concepts.name: IMDb sentiment dataset (raw aclImdb)
concepts.definition: Movie reviews labeled positive or negative by user rating, distributed as one text file per review in train/test × pos/neg folders, plus an unlabeled train/unsup folder.
concepts.intuition: A labeled pile of opinions, sorted into two boxes according to whether the reviewer liked the movie.
concepts.technical: The archive aclImdb_v1.tar.gz from ai.stanford.edu. The labeled reviews are 25,000 for training and 25,000 for testing, each half positive and half negative (p.130). The unsup/ folder has another 25,000 unlabeled reviews (p.438).
concepts.significance: The single benchmark used to compare every text model in chapter 14 and the Transformer classifier in chapter 15.
concepts.example: train/pos/ holds files of reviews with high ratings; test/neg/ holds held-out low-rated reviews.
concepts.misconception: That unsup/ is a third class. It is unlabeled data and must not be loaded as a category.

concepts.name: Unlabeled data
concepts.definition: Examples without target labels, here the reviews in unsup/.
concepts.intuition: Extra reading material with no answer key.
concepts.technical: It cannot be used directly for supervised loss computation, but it can drive self-supervised objectives such as predicting a word from its context, which is how word embeddings are pretrained.
concepts.significance: It is ignored for classification here, and reused later for embedding pretraining (p.438).
concepts.example: 25,000 IMDb reviews with no pos/neg assignment.
concepts.misconception: That unlabeled data is worthless for a classification problem.

concepts.name: Inspecting the data before modeling
concepts.definition: The practice of looking at raw samples before designing or training a model.
concepts.intuition: Tasting the ingredients before writing the recipe.
concepts.technical: Print a few examples per class, check lengths and encodings, look for markup or label noise.
concepts.significance: The authors stress that it grounds your intuition about what the model is actually doing, for text as much as for images.
concepts.example:
Opening a review file and noticing `
` HTML tags that a standardizer should strip.
concepts.misconception: That it is a beginner's step you can skip once you are experienced.

code.title: Downloading the IMDb movie review dataset
code.original_code:
import os, pathlib, shutil, random

zip_path = keras.utils.get_file(
    origin="https://ai.stanford.edu/~amaas/data/sentiment/aclImdb_v1.tar.gz",
    fname="imdb",
    extract=True,
)

imdb_extract_dir = pathlib.Path(zip_path) / "aclImdb"
code.what_it_does: Downloads the raw IMDb archive from Stanford, caches it under `~/.keras/datasets/`, extracts it, and builds a `pathlib.Path` pointing at the top-level `aclImdb` folder.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports the standard-library modules used in this listing and the next: `pathlib` for path arithmetic, and `os`, `shutil` and `random` for shuffling and moving files into a validation split (Listing 14.10, p.421). `keras` is assumed to be imported already.

`keras.utils.get_file` downloads the file from `origin` if it is not already cached, saving it under the name `fname="imdb"` in the Keras cache directory. `extract=True` unpacks the tar.gz. The returned path (stored as `zip_path`, although the archive is a gzipped tarball, not a zip) points at the extracted location.
The archive's contents sit in an `aclImdb/` folder, so it is appended with pathlib's `/` operator to get the dataset root.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: a URL. Output: the files on disk under `~/.keras/datasets/aclImdb/` and a `Path` object `imdb_extract_dir`.
code.algorithm: Check the cache; download if needed; extract the archive; return the path.
code.theory_link: This is the first step of a raw-text pipeline. Unlike `keras.datasets.imdb.load_data` (p.130), nothing is tokenized yet.

parameters.name: fname
parameters.role: Local name for the cached download.

parameters.name: extract
parameters.role: If True, unpack the archive after downloading.

pitfalls: The archive is roughly 80 MB compressed and much larger once extracted, so the first run needs network access and some disk space.
Beyond the book: the exact path returned by `get_file` with `extract=True` has changed between Keras versions. If `imdb_extract_dir` does not exist, print `zip_path` and adjust the path.
The variable name `zip_path` is just a name; the file is a .tar.gz.

code.title: Listing the dataset's directory structure
code.original_code:
>>> for path in imdb_extract_dir.glob("*/*"):
...     if path.is_dir():
...         print(path)
~/.keras/datasets/aclImdb/train/pos
~/.keras/datasets/aclImdb/train/unsup
~/.keras/datasets/aclImdb/train/neg
~/.keras/datasets/aclImdb/test/pos
~/.keras/datasets/aclImdb/test/neg
code.what_it_does: Iterates over every entry exactly two levels below `aclImdb/` and prints the ones that are directories, showing the split/label layout.

line_explanations.explanation: `glob("*/*")` matches paths of the form `<anything>/<anything>` relative to the root, such as `train/pos` and also top-level files' children.
Only directories are printed, so loose files (such as vocabulary or README files in the archive) are skipped.
Output: train has pos, unsup and neg; test has only pos and neg. The order reflects the filesystem's listing order, not a sort.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: `imdb_extract_dir`. Output: five printed directory paths.
code.theory_link: This shows that labels are encoded by directory, which directory-based dataset loaders rely on.
pitfalls: Your printed paths will show your real home directory and may appear in a different order.
Loading `train/` directly with a directory-based loader would pick up `unsup` as a third class.

deeper.title: Why order-agnostic models work so well for sentiment
deeper.body: Beyond the book: sentiment is carried largely by **which** words appear ('masterpiece', 'awful', 'waste'). A linear classifier over word presence can weight each word's evidence and add it up, which captures most of the signal. Order matters for negation ('not good') and for contrast ('the first half was dull, but…'), and that is where bigrams (section 14.4.2) and sequence models (section 14.5) can help. This explains why the authors say *both* approaches remain relevant.

deeper.title: The raw-text pipeline you are about to build
deeper.body:
1. **Download and extract** (Listing 14.8, this page).
2. **Inspect** a sample (Listing 14.9, p.421).
3. **Split** 20% of training files into a validation directory, ignoring `unsup/` (Listing 14.10, p.421).
4. **Load** `Dataset` objects with `text_dataset_from_directory` (p.421–422).
5. **Vectorize** with a tokenizer or `TextVectorization`, then train a set model (section 14.4) or a sequence model (section 14.5).

deeper.title: Labels from folders: a filing-cabinet analogy
deeper.body: Think of the dataset as a filing cabinet. One drawer is labeled *train*, another *test*; inside each there are folders marked *pos* and *neg*. Nobody wrote the label on the documents themselves; you learn a review's label from the folder it is in. The *unsup* folder is a stack of documents nobody has sorted yet.

questions.question: According to the page, when did interest in sequence models for NLP start rising?
options: In the 1990s, with the invention of LSTMs
In 2015, with the rebirth of RNNs
questions.answer: In 2015, with the rebirth of RNNs
questions.explanation: The text says interest in sequence models 'only started rising in 2015, with the rebirth of RNNs.' LSTMs date from the 1990s but did not trigger that rise; the Transformer came later; AlexNet is a computer-vision milestone.

questions.question: What does the `unsup/` directory contain, and why must it be excluded when building the labeled training set?
questions.answer: Reviews the dataset creator deliberately left unlabeled (they may be positive or negative). A directory-based loader would otherwise treat `unsup` as a third class.
questions.explanation: The page defines unsup/ as unlabeled reviews; p.421 ignores them for now, and p.438 later uses them for pretraining.

questions.question: How does the IMDb data used on this page differ from the version used in chapter 4, and what extra work does that create?
questions.answer: Chapter 4's version was prevectorized: reviews were already integer word-index sequences with a fixed vocabulary. Here you get raw text files, so you must read files, take labels from folders, split off validation data, choose a tokenizer and vectorize.
questions.explanation: The page contrasts the prevectorized chapter 4/5 data with raw text 'just like you would do when approaching a new text-classification problem in the real world' (see also p.130).

questions.question: What does `extract=True` do in `keras.utils.get_file` in Listing 14.8?
options: It unpacks the downloaded archive after downloading
It splits off a validation set
questions.answer: It unpacks the downloaded archive after downloading
questions.explanation: `extract=True` makes get_file unpack the tar.gz so the aclImdb folder appears on disk. Tokenization, validation splitting and ignoring unsup all happen in later steps.

questions.question: Why might a bag-of-words model, which ignores word order, still be a strong choice for movie-review sentiment?
questions.answer: Much of the sentiment signal comes from which words appear ('awful', 'brilliant'), so presence alone is very informative. Order mainly helps with negation and contrast.
questions.explanation: The page says both approaches remain relevant. The explanation of why is our own reasoning and is tested empirically in sections 14.4 and 14.5.

questions.question: How are review labels stored in the raw aclImdb dataset?
options: In a CSV file of filename,label pairs
As the first line of each review file
By the directory the file is in (pos/ or neg/)
They are not available; the dataset is unlabeled
questions.answer: By the directory the file is in (pos/ or neg/)
questions.explanation: Low-rated reviews were sorted into neg/ and high-rated ones into pos/. There is no separate label file, and only unsup/ is unlabeled.
